newsitem.title: GERMANY: Attempts to revive German jobs pact face hurdles.
newsitem.headline: Attempts to revive German jobs pact face hurdles.

text.p: German government, opposition and business leaders on Tuesday still sharply disagreed on how to fight record unemployment, even as new willingness to cooperate emerged before the Christmas holiday.

Realising that economic growth alone will not solve Germany's problem of record joblessness, politicians, trade unionists and business executives said Monday they wanted to revive talks on a failed "Alliance for Jobs."
But few of them on Tuesday offered new ideas about how to reach a consensus on the eve of a two-day holiday.

"The actual readiness of the players is certainly small. The insistence on their own principles is too large," the daily Berliner Zeitung wrote. "None of the sides showed anything that could come close to a whiff of a patent recipe."
Meanwhile, members of Chancelllor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition reiterated their belief in lower taxes, social spending and labour costs as the keys to economic recovery and job creation.

Only through greater use of part-time work can the Alliance for Jobs reach its goal of halving unemployment be the year 2000, Federal Labour Office president Bernhard Jagoda told Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
Otto Graf Lambsdorff, an economic expert for the Free Democrats, the coalition's junior partner, also told the same daily Bonn's 50-point austerity program "is aimed in the right direction."
Unions and opposition Social Democrats have protested Bonn's proposed spending cuts for months, and oppose widespread use of part-time work.
Meanwhile, regional newspapers called for more flexibility from Bonn and from employers.
"The Kohl government is missing the courage for softening its stance. This government is a prisoner of its solution: tax reductions," the Cologne Stadt-Anzeiger wrote in an editorial.

The Rhein-Neckar Zeitung blamed high unemployment, which is expected to reach 4.5 million early next year, on corporate concentration on cost-cutting and export markets. High jobless levels will last "until politicians and employers recognize that cars don't buy cars. People need jobs."

Hans Peter Stihl, head of the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), on Monday spoke out for new cooperation, saying employers must be ready to compromise on the volatile issue of cutting sick pay.
A Kohl spokesman said Bonn also is "ready to talk."
The alliance originally collapsed as businesses took tough lines in wage negotiations and Bonn backed a law making it possible to cut sick pay to 80 percent percent of normal wages.
